orders.explanation: Transcript 1 demonstrates deep understanding of the Django codebase, methodically locates the serializer, crafts and tests a fix, updates documentation, and verifies behavior across edge cases and the full test suite. Transcript 2 attempts only a partial fix and doesn’t complete the required test and doc updates. Therefore, Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 succinctly pinpoints the faulty `EnumSerializer`, applies the minimal code change to use `EnumClass[name]`, adds appropriate docs, and demonstrates thorough end-to-end verification. Transcript 1, by contrast, gets mired in test editing and incomplete refactoring, showing less direct problem-solving.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a complete, accurate investigation of the Django codebase, locates the exact upstream commits, applies the correct upstream fix, updates tests and docs, and verifies all relevant tests pass. Transcript 2 attempts a custom patch but never reaches a correct, fully verified solution.

Transcript 1 shows deep understanding of Django internals, uses code searches, constructs and applies a precise patch, and thoroughly tests the fix. Transcript 2 only lists files and logs without implementing or validating any solution. Clearly Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 provides a complete root-cause analysis, a precise patch to exclude unique constraints when deleting index_together, adds a regression test, and verifies the fix end-to-end. Transcript 2 only begins exploratory file listings and does not resolve the issue.

Transcript 1 methodically locates the bug in BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor, applies the precise patch to exclude unique constraints when deleting index_together, and verifies it with standalone reproductions, unit tests, and an end-to-end migration. Transcript 2 is incomplete and does not arrive at the full fix.

Transcript 1 methodically locates the relevant code, crafts a minimal upstream-style patch to use total_unique_constraints, verifies with both unit tests and the full Django test suite, and cleanly reverts test changes. Transcript 2 takes a more ad hoc approach by adding a new API, fails to run all existing tests, and leaves incomplete changes.

Transcript 2 is more concise and focused, making the minimal change to `in_bulk()`, directly consulting `total_unique_constraints` and validating with targeted reproduction scripts and full Django test suites. Transcript 1 is overly verbose, adds unnecessary helper methods, and meanders through shell commands without a clear, minimal fix.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deep, systematic investigation: it locates the relevant tests and Sphinx source, identifies the upstream fix commit, applies the precise patch, and verifies all related tests pass. Transcript 2 is much more superficial and fails to implement or verify the feature.

Transcript 2 quickly locates the official upstream fix commit in the Sphinx repository, extracts and cleanly applies the exact patch, and verifies the feature with tests. Transcript 1 instead reimplements the change manually in a verbose and error-prone manner.

Transcript 1 systematically traced the bug to the `split(None, 1)` call, located the upstream fix commit, applied the minimal `rsplit(None, 1)` patch, updated the CHANGES entry, and ran the full test suite to verify no regressions. Transcript 2 instead attempted a complex helper‐function patch with repeated insertion failures and did not demonstrate proper verification or alignment with the official fix.

Transcript 2 quickly pinpoints the exact upstream commit, applies the single-line change from split() to rsplit(), updates CHANGES, and verifies with tests. Transcript 1, by contrast, overengineers a custom parser and makes sprawling edits rather than using the much simpler, correct fix.

Transcript 1 is far more thorough and robust, handling environment detection, service startup without systemd, SSH user setup, permission edge-cases, full end-to-end testing over real SSH (including fallback from sudo to runuser), clean resets, and even a convenient restart script. Transcript 2 follows a simpler, more error-prone plan without those refinements or comprehensive testing.

Transcript 2 is far more thorough and robust: it handles system differences (no systemd, missing sudo), sets up SSHD and a user account, configures safe.directory and permissions, tests the workflow over a real SSH connection, fixes hook edge cases, cleans up and provides a startup script. Transcript 1 works but is much simpler and less complete.

Transcript 1 shows a far more systematic, knowledgeable approach—identifying and installing missing libraries, rebuilding John the Ripper for the host CPU, diagnosing cgroup CPU limits, optimizing cracking parameters, and maintaining a clear plan. Transcript 2 is more haphazard, struggles with dependencies, and resorts to a brute-force Python loop.

Transcript 2 demonstrates deeper system‐level expertise—diagnosing CPU feature mismatches, managing cgroup limits, installing and configuring build dependencies, rebuilding John correctly, and methodically tuning parallel cracking—whereas Transcript 1 resorts to a brute‐force Python loop without such sophisticated tool integration. Transcript 2’s structure and advanced troubleshooting indicate a more capable model.

Transcript 1 provides an in-depth root-cause analysis (examining libstdc++ patches, gdb backtraces, heap interactions, static initialization order) and crafts a precise, minimal fix that is fully verified with Valgrind. Transcript 2 is a much briefer, higher-level patch without the same detailed justification or rigorous validation.

Transcript 2 shows far deeper analysis of the custom libstdc++ patches, uses gdb and disassembly to pinpoint the facet‐registration bug, crafts an optimization-safe warm-up to trigger the library’s own virtual num_put path, and rigorously re-verifies with valgrind. This level of debugging and tailored fix demonstrates the more capable model.

Transcript 1 is clearly more focused and demonstrates a deep, correct analysis: it identifies the exact probability-1 differential, implements a fast in-Python f_function, writes a clean attack module, and thoroughly tests it. Transcript 2 is long, meandering through incorrect differential experiments and only converges at the end without a clear summary.

Transcript 1 shows a far more thorough, systematic differential analysis—testing many input differences, tracing state differences across rounds, empirically verifying probability-1 differentials, and ultimately constructing and validating a full attack script. Transcript 2 is much briefer and less complete.

Transcript 1 methodically pinpoints the CRLF injection issue (CWE-93), applies a minimal, correct fix to `_hkey` and `_hval`, produces the required report, and verifies all tests pass. Transcript 2 over-engineers the solution by trying to replace pickle with JSON for cookies, breaks existing tests, and fails to complete.

Transcript 2 quickly identifies the specific CWE-93 vulnerability, provides a concise patch for _hkey/_hval, generates a correct report.jsonl, and verifies all tests pass with minimal but sufficient detail. Transcript 1 wanders through unrelated pickle fixes and CRLF tests before converging, indicating less focused reasoning.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it planned and executed the entire setup correctly on the first try—creating the git user, configuring SSH, writing a concise post-receive hook, generating a proper self-signed certificate with SANs, configuring Nginx correctly, and verifying end-to-end functionality (including timing) with clean resets. Transcript 2 instead repeatedly encountered errors (host key issues, missing rsync, nginx misconfigurations, permission problems) and required multiple rounds of debugging and manual fixes.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a clear, systematic setup without repeated failures or ad hoc fixes. It configures the bare repo default branch, writes a precise hook, generates the certificate with SAN, configures Nginx correctly on the first try, measures deployment timing, and resets to a clean state—unlike Transcript 1, which required multiple iterations to fix rsync, alias, and permissions issues. ANSWER: 2

Transcript 1 implements a fully optimized C extension with analytic 2×2 solvers, raw LAPACK calls, and inverse iteration, achieving a 3–7× speedup over the reference. Transcript 2 simply calls numpy.linalg.eig with no optimization.

Transcript 1 shows a deep, systematic exploration of performance trade-offs, culminating in a custom C extension with LAPACK calls, inverse iteration, residual checks, and fallback handling. Transcript 2 merely uses numpy.linalg.eig with no optimization efforts. Clearly the more capable model is the one in Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far more sophisticated, cost-model-driven DP batching approach with Lagrangian tuning, multi-phase solver refinements, surgical p95 management, and thorough validation. Transcript 2 resorts to a simpler greedy grouping by gen_len range. The depth and rigor of Transcript 1 mark it as the more capable model.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model; it carries out a full end-to-end development cycle—data inspection, cost-model-based DP batching, parameter tuning, surgical p95 enforcement, final plan writing and validation—whereas Transcript 2 never completes the plan and gets stuck mid-tuning.

Transcript 1 presents a clear, systematic walkthrough: inspecting the environment, authoring a minimal custom mailman.cfg, configuring and launching Mailman, creating the list with the correct policy, updating Postfix maps, and then rigorously testing each flow (direct delivery, join, leave, post) and finally running the provided eval script to confirm success. Transcript 2, by contrast, is disorganized, repeatedly misconfigures Postfix/local delivery, resorts to trial-and-error hacks (procmail), and never arrives at a clean, reproducible solution.

Transcript 1 shows a complete, end-to-end setup: it writes and validates the Mailman configuration, starts Mailman, creates the list, sets the open subscription policy, configures Postfix’s transport and recipient maps, iterates through and fixes delivery issues (including mailbox formats and procmail), and finally passes all `/app/eval.py` tests. Transcript 2 only introspects the environment without performing the required configuration steps or verifying the solution.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper planning, systematic environment setup (installing missing tools only when needed), rigorous pattern inference with a dynamic Python prototype, extensive randomized and end‐to‐end verification, and a clean two‐parent merge with detailed commit history. Transcript 2 is more ad‐hoc, leaves junk files, only runs the explicit examples, and lacks the same thoroughness.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a higher level of planning and sophistication: it maintains an explicit plan, installs and configures tools only when needed, infers the mapping rule in a generic way, writes a well-documented and self-contained `map` implementation, and then validates it with both the provided examples and extensive randomized tests. This thoroughness and generalization show it was produced by the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a much deeper and more robust solution—implementing big-integer Fibonacci to avoid overflow, carefully crafting the polyglot quoting to eliminate warnings under strict compilation flags, exhaustively testing against an independent checker for very large N, and explaining the trick in detail. Transcript 2 uses a simple long-long Fibonacci with no big-integer support and only minimal testing.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a much deeper level of expertise: it handles arbitrary‐precision Fibonacci with a big‐integer C implementation, avoids compiler warnings with a carefully balanced polyglot structure, rigorously cross-checks results against an independent base-10 checker, tests performance on very large N, and documents all the corner cases. Transcript 1 solves the basic task but only with 64-bit `long long`, minimal testing, and no concern for overflow or warnings.

Transcript 1 shows a much deeper, iterative approach—carefully inspecting the environment, installing missing dependencies, adapting thread settings to cgroup quotas, refining multi‐mask vs single‐mask calls for speed, clipping logits to a padded ROI, performing per-pixel global arbitration to guarantee disjoint masks, extensive edge‐case and scale testing, and finally validating correctness thoroughly. Transcript 2 sketches a simpler batched prompt pipeline without these robustness, performance, and validation enhancements.

Transcript 1 provides a highly detailed, step-by-step development process: environment setup, thorough testing, performance tuning (thread limits, batching), extensive validation (demo, edge, degraded, and scale tests), and multiple iterative improvements. Transcript 2 is partial and incomplete, with exploratory steps but no final workable script. Transcript 1 clearly demonstrates the capabilities of the more advanced model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper data exploration, uses rdflib to validate assumptions and counts, constructs precise nested subqueries for the >10-student filter, and thoroughly tests the final SPARQL query against the graph. Transcript 2, by contrast, fails to execute or verify its query, relies on ad hoc filters without validation, and misses key checks.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it systematically explored and validated the data (using rdflib and precise counts), wrote a concise, logically correct SPARQL query, and directly tested its results against the graph. Transcript 1 contained more trial-and-error tool usage, untested fixes, and redundant steps without verifying the final query execution.

Transcript 1 shows a deep, systematic profiling approach—inspecting timer breakdowns, testing contact disabling, evaluating solver/jacobian options with tight tolerances, and rigorously verifying zero contacts across seeds—leading to the optimal combination (dense+PGS solver + contact disable). Transcript 2 is a more trial-and-error exploration that ultimately only switches to PGS+Euler without the contact optimization or detailed justification. Hence Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 performs a deep, systematic profiling of every phase of the simulation, explores solver, integrator, jacobian, iteration and tolerance settings, verifies correctness across many random seeds, and arrives at a minimal, well-justified change that meets the 60% speed target. Transcript 2 is much briefer and less comprehensive in its search and validation.
